procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated February 26, 1965 of the Madras High Court in Writ Petitions Nos. 1321, 1456, 1495, 1496 and 1553 of 1964.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Respondents challenged the department's action by writ petitions filed in the High Court under Art. 226 of the Constitution praying that the articles seized should be returned. The High Court concluded that the search warrant for the residential house was defective. The High Court held that sub-sections (2), (3) and (4) of section 41 were unconstitutional as they were unreasonable restrictions on the fundamental rights guaranteed under Art. 19(1) (f) and (g) of the Constitution.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The State Government appealed the High Court's decision. The Supreme Court granted certificates for appeal. The State Government argued that s.41 authorised search and seizure; secondly, that the State Legislature was competent to enact s.41(4) under item 54 c-f list II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution; and thirdly, that the provisions in question did not offend Art. 19(1) (f) and (g) of the Constitution and were in any case protected by Art. 19(51 and (6).

directions: Anything recovered on the defective search must be returned.
Anything confiscated must also be returned.
Parties to bear their own costs in all the appeals.

issue.issue_text: Whether Section 41(2) of the Act confers the power of search, or is it limited to inspection?

facts: The High Court had previously held that Section 41(2) of the Act only provided for inspection and did not confer the power to search, viewing the two as distinct actions.
law: Section 41(2) of the Act provides that a dealer's accounts, goods, offices, shops, godowns, vessels, and vehicles shall be open to inspection.
The proviso to Section 41(2) states that "all searches under this sub-section" must be conducted in accordance with the Code of Criminal Procedure.
Section 41(3) of the Act grants an empowered officer the power to seize accounts if they have reason to suspect tax evasion.
application: The Supreme Court acknowledged that while the power to inspect does not generally include the power to search, the specific wording of Section 41(2) is different.

The Court reasoned that the combination of the power to inspect places (offices, shops, etc.) and the power to inspect items within those places (accounts, goods, etc.) together amounts to the power to enter and search those premises to find the items to be inspected.
The Court found this interpretation logical, as an officer would enter a business's premises for the purpose of finding all relevant accounts, not just those the dealer chooses to present.

The Court pointed to the proviso of sub-section (2), which explicitly mentions "searches under this sub-section," as direct textual evidence that the legislature intended for the main part of the sub-section to include the power of search.

Furthermore, the Court noted that the power to seize accounts under sub-section (3) would be impossible without a preceding search. Therefore, sub-section (3) supports the interpretation that sub-section (2) must include the power of search.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's view and held that Section 41(2), when read as a whole and in conjunction with its proviso and sub-section (3), confers the power of search and is not limited to mere inspection.

issue.issue_text: Whether sub-sections (2) and (3) of Section 41 are unconstitutional for being unreasonable restrictions on the right to hold property and to carry on trade.

facts: The High Court had previously struck down sub-sections (2) and (3) of Section 41 of the Madras General Sales Tax Act.

The High Court's reasoning was that these provisions were unreasonable restrictions on the fundamental rights to hold property and carry on a trade, primarily because it believed there were no adequate safeguards against the arbitrary use of search and seizure powers.
law: Article 19(1)(f) and (g) of the Constitution guarantee the right to hold property and to carry on any trade or business.
These rights can be subjected to 'reasonable restrictions' in the interest of the general public.
Section 41(2) of the Act pertains to the power of search.
Section 41(3) of the Act pertains to the power to seize and retain account books.
application: The Supreme Court disagreed with the High Court's assessment and found that both sub-sections contained sufficient safeguards to make the restrictions reasonable.

Regarding sub-section (2) (the power to search), the Court held that the power was not arbitrary. It found that safeguards provided in the Code of Criminal Procedure apply to searches conducted under this sub-section. Given the objective of preventing tax evasion, the Court deemed the restriction reasonable.
Regarding sub-section (3) (the power to seize accounts), the Court identified several specific safeguards:
1. The officer must have a 'reason to suspect' that a dealer is evading tax.
2. The officer must record these reasons in writing *before* seizing the accounts.
3. The dealer must be given a receipt for the seized items at the time of seizure.
4. The accounts can only be retained for as long as is necessary for examination or inquiry.
5. An additional safeguard in the proviso limits retention to 30 days at a time, requiring permission from a higher officer for any extension.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that these built-in safeguards were sufficient to prevent the arbitrary use of power. Therefore, the restrictions imposed by sub-sections (2) and (3) of Section 41 on the rights to hold property and carry on trade were reasonable and constitutional. The Court explicitly disagreed with and overturned the High Court's finding on this issue.

issue.issue_text: Whether the search conducted was illegal due to non-compliance with the safeguards provided in Section 165 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

facts: A search was conducted by authorities who believed that the safeguards provided in Section 165 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) did not apply to their actions.
Consequently, the safeguards laid out in Section 165 of the CrPC were not followed during the search.
law: The Supreme Court disagreed with the High Court's assumption that Section 165 of the CrPC was inapplicable.
The Court held that a proviso in the relevant law explicitly states that all searches must be conducted, as far as possible, in accordance with the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

Therefore, the Court ruled that the safeguards contained in Section 165 of the CrPC—such as the requirement for an officer to have reasonable grounds, record those grounds in writing, and specify the thing being searched for—are applicable to the search in question.
application: The Court observed that because the authorities mistakenly believed Section 165 did not apply, they failed to follow its mandatory safeguards when conducting the search.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that since the safeguards provided in Section 165 of the Code of Criminal Procedure were not followed, the search was defective and illegal. As a result, the Court ordered that anything recovered from this search must be returned.

issue.issue_text: Whether the warrant for the search of the residential accommodation was invalid due to the Magistrate's non-application of mind.

facts: A search warrant for a residential accommodation was issued by a Magistrate on a printed form.
The Magistrate failed to strike out portions of the form that were not applicable.
The Magistrate also failed to fill in gaps in the form that should have been completed before issuance.
application: The High Court first examined the warrant and concluded that the failure to strike out irrelevant sections and fill in necessary gaps demonstrated that the Magistrate had not applied their mind to the necessity of the search.
The Supreme Court reviewed the High Court's decision.
While the Supreme Court disagreed with the High Court on other legal interpretations, it accepted the finding regarding the warrant's invalidity.
The Supreme Court referred to the warrant as "defective" in its own reasoning.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the High Court's conclusion that the search warrant was invalid. It held that the Magistrate's failure to properly complete the printed form showed a non-application of mind, and therefore, anything recovered from the search based on this defective warrant had to be returned.

issue.issue_text: Whether sub-section (4) of Section 41, which provides for seizure and confiscation, is valid.

facts: The validity of sub-section (4) of Section 41 of the Madras General Sales Tax Act, which authorized the seizure and confiscation of goods, was challenged.
The High Court had previously struck down this sub-section, finding it was beyond the legislative competence of the State.
Sub-section (4) contained a second proviso, added by a 1961 amendment, which included a clause (a).
law: A provision within a statute can be struck down if it is found to be repugnant to the entire scheme of the Act.
The doctrine of severability determines whether an invalid part of a statute can be removed while leaving the rest of the statute intact.
If an invalid provision is not severable, the entire section or statute it is part of must be struck down.
application: The Supreme Court agreed with the High Court's conclusion to strike down sub-section (4), but for entirely different reasons.

The Court's reasoning focused on clause (a) of the second proviso to sub-section (4). It found this clause to be "repugnant to the entire scheme of the Act" because it provided for the recovery of tax even before the taxable event (the first sale in the State) had occurred.
The Court then considered whether this repugnant proviso could be severed, leaving the main part of sub-section (4) in force.

It concluded that the proviso was not severable. The Court reasoned that because the legislature added this compulsory proviso at a later date, it clearly intended for the main part of the section and the proviso to operate together.
Therefore, the Court found it could not hold that the legislature intended for the main part of sub-section (4) to stand by itself without the proviso.
reasoning.conclusion: Because the repugnant second proviso was not severable from the main part of the sub-section, the Supreme Court held that the entire sub-section (4), along with its provisos, must fall and be struck down.

arguments.issue_text: Whether Section 41(2) of the Act confers the power of search, or is it limited to inspection?
appellant_arguments: Section 41 of the Act authorised search and seizure.
respondent_arguments: On a proper construction, Section 41 does not confer the power of search and is limited to inspection.

arguments.issue_text: Whether sub-sections (2) and (3) of Section 41 are unconstitutional for being unreasonable restrictions on the right to hold property and to carry on trade.
appellant_arguments: The provisions did not offend Article 19(1)(f) and (g) of the Constitution and were protected by Article 19(5) and (6).
respondent_arguments: Sub-sections (2) and (3) are unconstitutional as they are unreasonable restrictions on the right to hold property and to carry on trade.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the search conducted was illegal due to non-compliance with the safeguards provided in Section 165 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
appellant_arguments: The safeguards provided under Section 165 of the Code of Criminal Procedure were not applicable to the search.
respondent_arguments: The search was defective and illegal because the safeguards provided in Section 165 of the Code of Criminal Procedure were not followed.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the warrant for the search of the residential accommodation was invalid due to the Magistrate's non-application of mind.
appellant_arguments: The warrant for the search was valid.
respondent_arguments: The warrant for the search of the residential accommodation was defective and invalid.

arguments.issue_text: Whether sub-section (4) of Section 41, which provides for seizure and confiscation, is valid.
appellant_arguments: The State Legislature was competent to enact Section 41(4) under item 54 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution.
The power to seize and confiscate goods is ancillary and incidental to the power to tax, as it is necessary to check evasion.
respondent_arguments: The power of confiscation provided by sub-section (4) was not within the competence of the State Legislature under item 54, List II, of the Seventh Schedule.

cases.case_name: State of Rajasthan v. Leela Jain
cases.principle: For the general principle of construction that the function of a proviso is to limit the main part of the section and carve out something which but for the proviso would be part of the section itself.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A statutory power to search is a reasonable restriction on the right to hold property and carry on trade if it incorporates procedural safeguards, such as those in the Code of Criminal Procedure. However, if a search is conducted without following those incorporated procedural safeguards, the search is defective, and anything recovered or confiscated as a result must be returned.
obiter: The general question of whether a power to confiscate goods found during a search that are not in a dealer's account books is an ancillary power necessary to stop tax evasion was not decided.
The proper course for statutory construction is to construe a section or enactment as a whole, with each portion, including any proviso, throwing light on the rest.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The final order of the High Court allowing the writ petitions must stand, though the Supreme Court does not agree with the High Court's interpretation that Section 41(2) does not confer the power of search or that sub-sections (2) and (3) are unconstitutional. The appeal is dismissed because the search itself was illegal due to non-compliance with mandatory procedural safeguards, and the warrant for the residential search was defective, thus requiring the return of all seized and confiscated items.
legal_tests_applied: Reasonable Restriction Test: The court assessed whether the restrictions imposed by the search and seizure provisions on the fundamental rights to hold property and carry on trade under Article 19(1)(f) and (g) were reasonable. The test was met if sufficient procedural safeguards were in place to prevent arbitrary action, keeping in view the legislative object of preventing tax evasion.
why_appellant_lost: The search was rendered illegal because the officers failed to follow the mandatory procedural safeguards of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The court reasoned: 'as the safeguards provided in s. 165 of the Code of Crimina I Procedure were not followed, anything recovered on a defective search of this kind must be returned.'

The warrant for the search of the residential accommodation was defective, invalidating any recovery made under it. The court concluded: 'anything recovered from the search of the residential accommodation on the basis of this defective warrant must be· returned.'

The power of confiscation under Section 41(4) was held to be invalid because it was repugnant to the scheme of the Act, as it compelled the recovery of tax before the taxable event (the first point of sale) could have occurred. The court stated: 'As such it was repugnant to the entire scheme of the Act and sub-section (4) must therefore be struck down.'
why_respondent_won: The search was procedurally flawed and therefore illegal, mandating the return of seized items. The court found: 'the safeguards provided under s.165 of the Code of Criminal Procedure do not appear to have been fellowed when the search was made for the simple reason that everybody thought that that provision was not applicable'.

The warrant authorizing the search of the residential premises was invalid, leading to the court's direction that 'anything recovered from the search of the residential accommodation on the basis of this defective warrant must be· returned.'
The statutory provision for confiscation, Section 41(4), was struck down as invalid, leading to the order that 'anything confiscated· must also be returned, as we have held that sub-s.(4) must fall.'
policy_considerations: The court balanced the state's objective of preventing tax evasion against the citizens' fundamental rights, holding that a restriction is reasonable 'keeping in view the object of the search, namely, prevention of evasion of tax.'

The necessity of procedural safeguards to prevent arbitrary use of power was emphasized, as the court noted that the application of the Code of Criminal Procedure to searches 'clearly show that the power to search under sub-s.(2) is not arbitrary.'

The court considered the practicalities of administration, reasoning that empowering officers who are not of the highest rank to conduct searches is not inherently unreasonable, as 'if searches could only be made by high officers there would not be enough officers available to do so... the Government will see that o(ficers of proper statas are empowered.'
